unit.title: Use social media tools for collaboration and engagement

summary: This unit teaches you to use social media and online tools at work: to present a business well, win and keep customers, and work with a team in different places. You will learn to set up and secure a business profile, respect privacy, consent and copyright, plan and create good posts, reply to customers and complaints, use group chats, shared documents, calendars, cloud storage and video calls, and use insights to see what is working.

blocks.p: Most Jamaican customers now find a tradesperson, salon, spa or restaurant on their phone, and most work teams keep in touch through group chats and shared files. Used well, these tools bring in business at low cost and save time. Used carelessly, they leak private information, let scammers in and damage a business's name in public. This unit is shared by several programmes, so the examples come from electrical contractors, salons, spas, bakeries, restaurants and the Centre itself.

blocks.note: Practise on the Centre's practice accounts or in a document, and publish nothing in a business's name unless your instructor or employer says so. Use made-up names, or real people only with their written consent.

blocks.h: Benefits and limits for a small business

head: Benefits
Limits and risks
rows: Reaches many people quickly and at low cost
Photos and videos show the work better than words
Customers can share posts with friends
Two-way contact: questions and bookings at any time
Results can be measured
Needs regular time and care
Mistakes and complaints are seen in public
Scams, hacking and privacy risks
Not every customer uses it: some older people, or people with little data
A post seen by many people is not always a sale

head: Method
Good for
Weak points
rows: Social media and messaging
Fast, cheap, visual, shareable, measurable
Needs steady work; public complaints; misses people who are not online
Phone call
Personal, urgent or detailed matters, such as confirming a job or calming a complaint
Slow; one person at a time; no written record unless you make one
Printed flyer or notice
People in the area who are not online
Costs money to print; cannot be changed; hard to know if it worked
Radio or newspaper advert
Wide local reach
Costly; hard to measure; one-way

blocks.p: Most small businesses do best with a **mix**: social media for showing work and staying in touch, the phone for personal and urgent matters, and print for people who are not online.

sections.title: Setting up a business profile and keeping it secure

head: Include
Leave out
rows: Business name and logo
Services and, where useful, prices in J$
Area served (for example 'Clarendon and Manchester')
Opening hours
Business phone, business email and a link to book or to the website
A short, plain description
Staff home addresses and personal phone numbers
Customers' names or what they bought
Bank details, passwords or card numbers
Anything you would not want a stranger to know

ul: Create the account with a **business email address** that the business controls, not a staff member's personal email. If that person leaves, the business must not lose its page.
Keep **business and personal accounts separate**. Personal posts do not belong on the business page, and the business should not depend on one person's private account.
Use the business's logo and a clear photo; keep the name the same on every platform so customers can find it.
Use a **long passphrase**: three or more random words with numbers and symbols, at least 12 characters, such as Mango7!Ladder?Blue. Not the business name, a birthday or 12345678.
Use a **different password for every account**. A password manager can remember them for you.
**Never share passwords** by text, chat or email. Give each staff member their own access instead (below).

blocks.p: **Two-step verification** (two-factor authentication) asks for a second check after the password, usually a short **verification code** sent by text or shown in an authenticator app. A thief who steals the password still cannot get in without the code. Turn it on for every business account, and keep the backup codes somewhere safe.

blocks.note: **Never give anyone a verification code**, whatever they say. A common trick is a message from a 'friend' or 'the platform': 'I sent you a code by mistake, please send it back.' That code is the key to your account.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Most business pages let you give each person their own **role**, such as admin, editor or moderator, logged in with their own account. Then nobody shares a password, and the owner can see who posted what.
Give each person only the access they need. Keep at least two trusted admins, so that the business is not locked out if one leaves.
Remove access at once when someone leaves the business.
Log out of shared computers, and lock your phone with a PIN or fingerprint.

head: Warning sign
Example
rows: Urgency or threats
'Your page will be disabled in 24 hours unless you verify now.'
A request for a password, a code or card details
'Log in here to confirm your account.'
A link to an odd web address
A login page whose address is slightly misspelt
Too good to be true
'You have won a free boost worth US$500.'
Poor spelling, strange greetings
'Dear valued page ownr'

blocks.p: Do not click the link or reply. Check any warning by opening the app yourself, not through the message, and tell your manager. **Malware** (harmful software such as viruses and spyware) often arrives the same way, through links and attachments.

flow: Change the password from a safe device, and turn on two-step verification
Log out all other sessions and remove anyone you do not recognise from the page roles
Check the recovery email and phone number have not been changed
Tell your manager, and report it to the platform through its help pages
Warn customers through other channels not to trust strange messages from the page
Check what was posted or sent while the account was out of your control

sections.title: Privacy, consent, copyright and your digital footprint

blocks.p: Customers' names, addresses, phone numbers, health details, photos and payments are private. **Jamaica's data protection law** expects businesses to keep personal information secure and use it only for the purpose it was given for. Never post or share it outside the people who need it, and keep it out of group chats that do not need it.

ul: Ask the person **before** you photograph or post them, their hair, nails or skin, or their home or property, and tell them where it will appear. Many businesses use a short written **consent form**.
For a child under 18, get the consent of a **parent or guardian** as well as the child's agreement.
Show only what is needed: the nails, the hairstyle, the finished distribution board. Leave out faces, house numbers, car number plates and street signs unless the person has agreed.
If a person later asks for a photo to be taken down, **take it down promptly** and tell them it has gone.
Use privacy settings to control who sees personal accounts and posts.

blocks.note: For electrical and security work, take extra care: a photo can show a customer's address, gate, alarm panel, camera positions or keys, which helps a burglar. Do not tag the customer's location, and post photos of their property only with their consent.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Photos, videos, music, writing and logos belong to the people who made them. **Do not post them as your own** or copy them without permission, even if they are 'all over the internet'.
Giving credit in a caption is not the same as having permission.
Use your own photos and videos, or ones the business has paid for or been given permission to use.
For music in videos, use the music library the platform offers for business use, or none. Popular songs added without a licence can get the post muted or removed.

blocks.p: Your **digital footprint** is the record of everything you post, like, share and comment on over time. Posts can be screenshotted and shared, even after you delete them. Employers, customers and the Centre may see them.

ul: Think before you post: would you be happy for your employer and your customers to see it?
Do not post complaints about your employer, customers or co-workers, or photos of customers' homes and jobs, on your personal pages.
Wearing your work uniform in a photo links the post to the business.
Follow your workplace's **social media policy**: who may post for the business, what may be shared, and how to handle complaints.

blocks.p: A **content calendar** is a plan of what will be posted, on which day and at what time, with its purpose and who will prepare it. Planning ahead keeps the page active, gives a good mix of posts, and leaves time to get photos, consent and approval.

head: Day and time
Purpose
Post idea (electrical contractor)
Who
rows: Mon 7 p.m.
Tip
Three signs an outlet is overloaded, with a photo
Tajay
Wed 12 noon
Show our work
A neat new panel in a Mandeville house (with consent)
Kirk
Fri 6 p.m.
Offer
Free safety check with every rewire booked this month
Tajay

ul: Mix the kinds of post: tips, finished work, behind the scenes, customer stories (with permission), offers and news.

Use Jamaican seasons and dates: back-to-school, the hurricane season (June to November) with storm safety tips, Emancipation and Independence in August, Heritage Week in October, Christmas, and Mother's Day and Valentine's Day for salons and spas.
**Schedule** posts in advance, so that they go out regularly at the times your followers are most active, even on busy days.
Use good light, ideally daylight; hold the phone steady; keep the lens clean.
Keep the background tidy: no rubbish, tools lying about or other customers.
Show the finished work clearly, close enough to see the quality.
**Show safe practice.** A photo of a worker on a metal ladder near wires, without safety glasses, or working in a live panel, tells customers the business is careless and can be copied by others.
Short videos (under about a minute) often get more attention than photos: a hairstyle being finished, bread coming out of the oven, a tidy panel being labelled.

flow: Say what the photo shows, in a short, plain, friendly sentence
Add useful information: the service, the area, the price in J$ if it is an offer, what it includes
Add a **call to action**: words that ask the reader to do something, such as 'Message us to book' or 'Call 876-555-0123 for a free quote'
Add two to five relevant hashtags, including the place (for example #HayesClarendon #ElectricalSafety)
Add alternative text to photos, and captions on videos, so that people with poor sight or hearing can follow

head: Check
Why
rows: Spelling and grammar
Mistakes make the business look careless.
Facts and prices
A wrong price or date causes arguments later.
Tone
Friendly and professional; no jokes about customers, rivals or co-workers.
Privacy and consent
No private details; consent for every person or property shown.
Safety
The photo shows safe work.
Approval
Your supervisor approves posts if the business requires it.

ul: A **sponsored (boosted) post** is paid for so that it is shown to more people, chosen by area, age or interests. Set a budget in J$ and an end date, and aim it at people who can actually use the business.

An **influencer** is a person with many followers who trust their views. If the business pays or gives free services to an influencer, the post must say so clearly, as the platforms' rules require. Choose people whose followers fit the business.

sections.title: Engaging with customers and handling complaints

blocks.p: **Engagement** is how people react to posts: reactions (likes), comments, **shares** (passing a post on to their own followers), saves, mentions and messages. Engagement shows that people are interested, and platforms show posts with more engagement to more people.

ul: Reply **quickly**, ideally within a few hours during opening hours. Customers who are answered fast feel valued and are more likely to book. Set an away message for after hours.
Be friendly and personal: use the customer's name, answer the actual question, and sign with your first name if the business does.
Thank people for kind comments with a short, warm reply.
Move bookings and anything private (addresses, payments, health details) into a **direct message** or a phone call.
Never argue in public, and never post a customer's private details, even to defend the business.

flow: Do not delete it or reply in anger; tell your supervisor and agree the response
Reply quickly in public: thank them, say sorry they are unhappy, and say you want to put it right
Invite them to continue privately, by direct message or phone
In private: listen, check the facts and agree what will be done
Do what was agreed, and follow up to check they are satisfied
If they agree, thank them in public for letting you put it right
Record the complaint and its cause, so the business can stop it happening again

head: Do
Don't
rows: Stay calm, polite and brief
Blame the customer or argue the details in public
Apologise for their experience
Copy and paste the same reply to everyone
Offer a private channel and a named person
Post their address, invoice or private messages
Keep the promise you make
Delete genuine complaints, which looks like hiding

ul: Reply to good and bad reviews. Other customers read the replies as well as the reviews.
**Never write fake reviews**, or ask friends and family to post them. They mislead customers, break the platforms' rules and can get the page penalised.
Do not offer discounts in exchange for a customer changing or removing a review.
Report reviews that are clearly fake, spam or abusive to the platform.

blocks.note: Some comments are abusive, threatening, hateful or spam. Do not reply in kind. Your supervisor decides, following the business's policy, whether to hide, delete or report them, and whether to block the account.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Tool
Use it to
Good practice
rows: Group chat
Share quick updates and questions with the team
Agree simple ground rules: work topics only, sensible hours, polite and short, no customers' private details. Use @mentions to reach one person.
Shared document
Write and edit one file together, at the same time, from anywhere
Each person writes in their own part; use comments or suggesting mode to propose changes to other people's text.
Version history
See who changed what and when, and bring back an earlier version
Restore an earlier version if something is deleted by mistake.
Shared calendar
Show bookings, shifts and meetings in one place
Create an event, invite people, add the place and a reminder; accept or decline invitations promptly.
Cloud storage
Keep files online, reachable from any device, and share folders
Use clear folder and file names; share only with the people who need it.
Video call
Meet face to face on screen and share a screen
Send an agenda; mute when not speaking; one person hosts, one takes notes.

head: Setting
Who can open the file
rows: Restricted (named people)
Only the people you add by name or email. **The safest choice for work files.**
Anyone with the link
Anyone who gets the link, including people it is forwarded to. Use with care, never for private information.
Public
Anyone, and it may show up in searches. Not for work files.

ul: Give each person the least access they need: **viewer** (read only), **commenter** (can add comments) or **editor** (can change the file).
Remove people's access when the work is finished or they leave the team.
If you cannot open a file someone shared, politely ask them to check the sharing settings.
Test your camera, microphone and connection before the call; use headphones in a noisy place.
Press **mute** when you are not speaking, so background noise does not drown out the speaker.
Video uses a lot of data. On mobile data, join on Wi-Fi where you can, or turn off your camera to save data.
Be on time, dress as you would for work, and keep to the agenda.

blocks.p: **Netiquette** means good manners when communicating online. Written messages have no tone of voice, so they are easily misunderstood, and they can be copied and forwarded.

ul: Be polite and professional: greet people and thank them.
Keep messages short, clear and on topic; check spelling before you send.
Do not write in ALL CAPITAL LETTERS: it looks like shouting.
Reply in good time, and send work messages at sensible hours, not late at night.
Do not forward other people's messages or photos without asking; think before you 'reply all'.
If you are upset, wait before you reply.

blocks.p: **Cyberbullying** is using online messages, posts or images to hurt, threaten, embarrass or exclude someone. Never take part, even by liking or sharing.

flow: Do not reply or hit back
Save the evidence: screenshots with the date and the account name
Block the account and report it to the platform
Tell your instructor, supervisor or someone you trust
For threats or serious abuse, report it to the police

blocks.note: If a co-worker posts something unkind about a customer or a colleague in a work chat, do not join in. Say it is not right if you can, and report it to your supervisor if it carries on.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Most business pages have an **insights** (analytics) section. It shows how posts are doing, so that the business can do more of what works and less of what does not.

head: Measure
What it tells you
rows: Reach
How many different people saw a post
Impressions (views)
How many times the post was shown, counting repeat views
Engagement (interactions)
Reactions, comments, shares, saves and clicks
Engagement rate
Interactions as a percentage of reach: how interesting people found the post
Followers
How many people follow the page, and how fast that is growing
Link clicks, calls and messages
How many people took the next step towards buying
Audience and active times
Where followers live, their age group, and when they are online

blocks.p: **Engagement rate = interactions ÷ reach × 100.** Example: a post reached 2,400 people and got 96 reactions, comments and shares. 96 ÷ 2,400 = 0.04, and 0.04 × 100 = **4%**. Platforms work this out in slightly different ways, so compare posts on the same platform.

flow: Set a simple goal, such as more booking messages each month
Compare the figures for different kinds of post over a few weeks
Find what works: the kind of post, the topic and the time of day
Do more of what works and change one thing at a time
Check again after a few weeks and keep a short record

ul: Look past likes to **real results**: messages, calls, bookings and sales. Ask new customers how they heard about the business, and note it.
A small number of keen followers in your area is worth more than many followers who live too far away to buy.

blocks.note: Insights show what happened, not why. Use them alongside what customers tell you, and what you know about your area and your season.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the main kinds of social media and collaboration tool and say what each is good for.

I can write a caption with a call to action and suitable hashtags, and check it before posting.
I can reply to comments and reviews and handle a complaint step by step.
I can use a group chat, shared document, shared calendar, cloud storage and video call with good netiquette.
I can choose safe sharing settings and access levels for files.
I can respond to cyberbullying correctly.
I can read insights, work out an engagement rate and decide what to change.

terms: Words in a post that ask the reader to do something, such as 'Book now'.
Keeping files online so that they can be reached from any device.
A person's agreement, given before their photo or details are used.
A plan of what will be posted, and when.
Using online messages or posts to hurt, threaten or embarrass someone.
The record of everything a person posts and does online over time.
How people react to posts: reactions, comments, shares, saves and clicks.
A word after the # sign that links posts on one topic.
A person with many followers who trust their views.
Figures that show how a page and its posts are doing.
Harmful software, such as a virus or spyware, that damages a device or steals information.
A message that tries to trick you into giving a password, code or payment details.
The number of different people who saw a post.
Passing a post on to your own followers.
A second check, such as a code, needed as well as the password to log in.
A record of the changes to a shared file, from which an earlier version can be restored.

c1.title: A business page for an electrical contractor in Hayes
c1.text: Mr Kirk Ellis runs a small electrical contracting business in Hayes, Clarendon, and asks trainee Tajay to set up a business page. Mr Ellis has been posting jobs from his personal account and wants to text his password to Tajay and another worker so they can post too. Tajay has some photos from last week's jobs, including one of a new panel with a co-worker in the background on an aluminium ladder, without safety glasses.

c2.title: Nail photos at a Half Way Tree nail bar
c2.text: Nail technician Shantae works at a nail bar in Half Way Tree, St Andrew, and posts photos and short videos of her designs on the business's page. Today her clients include a 15-year-old girl who came with her mother, and an adult client who loves her nails but does not want her face shown. Shantae wants to add a popular song to a short video of the designs.

c3.title: A one-star review for a Montego Bay AC and electrical service
c3.text: An air-conditioning and electrical service in Montego Bay, St James, gets a one-star review from Mr Dwight Samuels: 'Technician came three hours late and left dust all over my bedroom. Never again!' Trainee Romaine manages the page with the office manager, Mrs Simone Grant. The owner's nephew wants to reply 'You weren't even home when we came!' and to ask friends to post five-star reviews to push the bad one down.

c4.title: Planning a community workshop from Port Maria
c4.text: Six trainees at a training centre in Port Maria, St Mary, are planning a free community workshop on electrical safety and hurricane preparedness. Their team leader, Tasha, sets up a cloud storage folder, a shared planning document, a calendar event and a group chat, and they meet once a week by video call. Some members join the call from home on mobile data.

c5.title: Insights for a Brown's Town bakery
c5.text: A family bakery in Brown's Town, St Ann, posts on its page three times a week. Last month its photo posts each reached about 1,200 people and got about 30 interactions; its short videos of bread coming out of the oven each reached about 2,000 people and got about 120 interactions. The owner, Miss Joy Walters, wants more orders for Christmas cakes and has J$5,000 to boost one post.

questions.q: Which email address should Tajay use to create the business page?
o: Tajay's own personal email, as he will be the one posting
Mr Ellis's personal email, as he owns the business
A new free email account made just for this one page
A business email address that the business controls
questions.why: A business email that the business controls keeps the page safe if a staff member leaves or loses access to a personal account. It also keeps business and personal matters separate.

questions.q: Mr Ellis wants to text his password to Tajay and another worker. What should Tajay suggest instead?
o: Give each worker their own access to the page with a suitable role
Send the password by voice note instead, as it is harder to copy
Change the password to something easy that all three can remember
Write the password on a card and keep it in the work van's glovebox
questions.why: Page roles let each person log in with their own account, so no password is shared, each person's posts can be seen, and access can be removed when someone leaves. Passwords sent in messages or written down are easily stolen.

questions.q: Should Tajay post the photo of the new panel with his co-worker in the background?
o: Yes, as the panel is neat and the ladder is only in the background
Yes, but only with a caption explaining that the ladder was not used
No; post a photo that shows the work done safely and correctly
No; electrical work should never be shown on social media at all
questions.why: A photo of a metal ladder near electrical work and a worker without safety glasses tells customers the business is careless, and others may copy it. Retake the photo, or crop to the panel, so that only safe practice is shown.

questions.q: A follower sends the page a message: 'Sorry, I sent a 6-digit login code to you by mistake. Please send it back to me.' What should Tajay do?
o: Send it back politely, since the follower made an honest mistake
Send it back, but only after checking the follower's profile picture
Not send it: it is a trick to get the page's two-step login code
Post the code on the page, so that the follower can see it there
questions.why: The code was sent because someone is trying to log in to the page, and they need the code to finish. Never give a verification code to anyone. Tell Mr Ellis, and change the password if you think it may be known.

questions.q: Shantae wants to post a photo of the 15-year-old girl's nails, showing her face. What does she need first?
o: Her mother's consent as well as the girl's agreement
Only the girl's own agreement, since they are her nails
Nothing, because the girl is a customer of the nail bar
The owner's approval only, as the page belongs to the shop
questions.why: A child under 18 cannot give consent alone; a parent or guardian must agree as well as the child. Even then, show only what is needed: a photo of the nails alone may be better.

questions.q: How should Shantae deal with the adult client who does not want her face shown?
o: Post the photo anyway, as it is the nails that matter most
Tag the client by name so that people know whose nails they are
Post it, but only on the page's story so that it disappears
Show only her hands and nails, with nothing that identifies her
questions.why: Consent can be partial. Respect exactly what the client agreed to: photograph only her hands and nails, with no face, name, tag or other detail that identifies her.

questions.q: Shantae wants a popular song in her short video. What is the right approach?
o: Use any song, as long as the artist is named in the caption
Use only the first 30 seconds of the song, which is always allowed
Use music the platform offers for business use, or use no music
Use the song, since the nail bar paid to download it for the shop
questions.why: Music belongs to its owners, and naming the artist is not permission. Buying a song to play in the shop does not give the right to put it in posts. Use the platform's licensed music for business accounts, or none.

questions.q: A week later the adult client asks Shantae to remove the photo of her nails. What should Shantae do?
o: Take it down promptly and let the client know it has been removed
Keep it up, because the client agreed when the photo was taken
Keep it up but change the caption, so that the client is not named
Ask the client to pay a fee to cover the cost of taking it down
questions.why: People can change their minds about how their images are used. Taking the photo down quickly, and telling the client, respects her privacy and keeps her trust in the business.

questions.q: Which public reply to Mr Samuels is best?
o: 'Thanks for your feedback! We always aim to give great service.'
'Mr Samuels, we are sorry about the delay and the mess. Please message us so we can put it right.'
'We were late because of traffic on the Bogue road. That is not our fault, and the dust was minimal.'
'Mr Samuels, your job in Ironshore on 3 March was finished and you paid us J$28,000, so we did our part.'
questions.why: A good reply is quick, polite and personal: it apologises for his experience and offers a private channel to put it right. A copied reply ignores the complaint, arguing makes it worse, and posting his address and payment breaks his privacy.

questions.q: Why should Romaine and Mrs Grant refuse the nephew's plan to get friends to post five-star reviews?
o: Fake reviews mislead customers and break the platforms' rules
Five-star reviews from friends take too long to appear online
Only reviews from customers in St James are counted by the site
Too many good reviews make a business look too expensive to use
questions.why: Reviews are trusted because they come from real customers. Fake reviews deceive people, can get the page penalised, and destroy trust if they are found out. Answering the real complaint well does far more good.

questions.q: The office arranges a free return visit and Mr Samuels is happy. What should happen next?
o: Ask him to delete his review in exchange for a discount next time
Record the complaint and its cause, so it can be prevented
Report his review to the platform as fake, now that it is settled
Post his job sheet on the page to show that the work was finished
questions.why: Recording the complaint, such as poor timekeeping and no dust sheets, lets the business fix the cause. If he agrees, a short public thank-you shows other customers that problems are put right. Offering rewards to change reviews breaks platform rules.

questions.q: Later, another person posts a comment full of swear words about the technician. What should Romaine do?
o: Reply in the same strong words, so the business is not seen as weak
Delete every comment on the review, including Mr Samuels's own
Tell Mrs Grant, who decides whether to hide or report it
Post the technician's side of the story with his phone number
questions.why: Abusive comments are not answered in kind. The supervisor follows the business's policy to hide, delete or report them and block the account if needed, while genuine complaints stay and are answered.

questions.q: How should Tasha share the planning folder?
o: Make it public, so that the community can see the plan as it grows
Give everyone her own login so that they all use the same account
Turn on 'anyone with the link' and post the link in a parish group
Share it with each team member by name, with the access each needs
questions.why: Sharing with named people keeps the plan and any contact details private. Give each person the least access they need, such as editor for the planners and viewer for others. A public link can be forwarded to anyone.

questions.q: Two members want to propose changes to the safety section, which another member wrote, without overwriting her text. What should they use?
o: A new copy of the document saved with their own changes
Suggesting mode or comments in the shared document
The group chat, pasting in the whole section again
The calendar event, adding their changes as a note
questions.why: Suggesting mode (tracked suggestions) and comments show proposed changes to the writer, who can accept or reject them. Separate copies split the plan into versions that nobody can keep track of.

questions.q: During the weekly video call, members on mobile data keep freezing, and background noise drowns out the speaker. What should they do?
o: Mute when not speaking; use Wi-Fi or turn off video
Keep cameras on and microphones open so everyone feels included
Shout so that their voices come through over the background noise
Leave the call and send their views later by email to each person
questions.why: Muting stops background noise covering the speaker. Video uses a lot of data, so joining on Wi-Fi, or turning off the camera, keeps the call running smoothly and saves the members' data.

questions.q: How can Tasha make sure all six members have the workshop date and get a reminder?
o: Post the date once in the group chat and hope everyone sees it
Write the date on the classroom whiteboard on the next training day
Send a calendar invitation to each member, with a reminder
Phone each member, one at a time, the evening before the workshop
questions.why: A calendar invitation puts the event in each person's own calendar with the time and place, shows who has accepted, and sends reminders automatically. A chat message is easily lost among other messages.

questions.q: What is the engagement rate of the bakery's short videos?
questions.why: Engagement rate = interactions ÷ reach × 100 = 120 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 6%. The photo posts manage 30 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 2.5%, so the videos interest people more than twice as much.

questions.q: How can Miss Walters tell whether the posts are bringing in Christmas cake orders, not just likes?
o: Count the likes, since each like usually means one cake ordered
Track orders from the posts and ask buyers how they heard
Compare her number of followers with another bakery's page
Post more often, since more posts always bring in more orders
questions.why: Likes show interest, not sales. Counting the order messages that come from each post, and asking customers how they heard about the bakery, links the posts to real results she can plan with.

questions.q: Miss Walters will spend J$5,000 boosting one post about Christmas cakes. Which audience setting makes most sense?
o: Everyone in the world, to reach the largest number of people
People anywhere in the Caribbean who follow cake and baking pages
Only her existing followers, since they have already liked the page
People who live within easy reach of Brown's Town
questions.why: A boosted post works best when it reaches people who can actually buy. Aiming at people within easy travelling or delivery distance makes the J$5,000 bring in orders rather than likes from people who can never collect a cake.

questions.q: A trainee posts a video on his personal page laughing at a customer's old wiring, showing the outside of the house and the street. What is the main problem?
o: Videos of wiring should be posted only as stories that disappear
It is fine on a personal page, because the business page was not used
It is only a problem if the video gets more than a hundred views
It exposes a customer's home and harms the business's name
questions.why: The video identifies the customer's home, shares their private business without consent, and makes the trainee and his employer look unprofessional. Personal pages are part of a digital footprint; the video should come down and the supervisor be told.
